Allow me to use issues within the EU as a parallel.

Take the recent issues with Greece. Germany, who has a very strong economy, is essentially saying they don't want to spend the rest of forever subsidizing Greece's bad decisions. And Greece has definitely made some very bad decisions. Many feel like it's well within reason that Germany would want to stop paying out money they're never going to get back.

That's what happens in the US, though. Many of our states receive more in aid than they pay in taxes. That means they aren't profitable, and would be bankrupt on their own - they're subsidized by other states with stronger economies. So now, imagine if in the preceding paragraph, we replaced Germany with California and Greece with Alabama. The reason it works here, though, is because the federal government has the authority to overrule any truly bad decisions that 'taker' states make, to keep them from completely tanking the 'giver' states. There's no such political treaty in the EU, only a financial one, and that's why Greece is a crisis and Alabama is just how things work.

I'm using tax money here, because it's numbers, which makes it easy to measure and chart, but it's a principle that extends to every area of politics. Every state feeds resources into the union - money; but also people, time, labor, culture, and so forth - and every state receives something in return.

This is why education is a federal concern, and not just a state one. States with poor graduation rates and high teen pregnancy rates need doctors and teachers and lawyers just as badly as anywhere else, but they have to come from somewhere. By allowing poor educational standards, a state wastes its own resources in the form of smart young people, and creates a 'brain drain' on other states that made better decisions. It's intellectual welfare.

So yes, one of the great things about giving states some autonomy is it allows for 50 independent field laboratories, and for regional governments to make decisions that best represent the needs and values of their constituency - but when states stubbornly keep making bad choices based on ideas proven not to work, the rest of the nation suffers for them, and it places an unfair burden on the states that have to prop up the deficiencies.
